title: A missing wing part has frozen Boeing's 777 cargo plane line for nearly two months
subtitle: A fight with Vaero, the only maker of a wing rib kit, stalled the 777 freighter and slowed the 767. Here is what a sole supplier is and why it matters.
content_html:
Picture the factory line for one of the world's best-known cargo planes going quiet. Not because of a strike or a fire, but because one small company stopped sending one wing part. That is what has happened to Boeing's 777 freighter, a giant plane built only to carry goods.

On 24 October 2026, BusinessLine carried a Reuters report that a fight with a small Florida supplier has stopped production of the 777 freighter for nearly two months. It has also slowed work on the smaller 767, including its cargo version and the KC-46, a military plane that refuels other planes in the air.

Who is the supplier, and what is the part?

The supplier is a company called Vaero, based in Florida. The part is called a trailing-edge rib kit.

Here is what that means in simple words. The trailing edge is the back edge of a plane's wing. The rib pieces are frames inside the wing that hold its shape, a bit like the thin sticks inside a kite. Without them, the wing cannot be built.

In August, Boeing went to court. In its complaint, Boeing said Vaero had stopped delivering these rib kits, which stalled work at its wing factory in Everett, in the US state of Washington. That factory makes wings for both the 777 freighter and the 767. Boeing called the part "indispensable", which means it simply cannot do without it.

According to Law.com, which first reported the lawsuit on 27 August, Boeing claimed Vaero refused to deliver the parts unless Boeing paid tens of millions of dollars in extra money.

What is a sole supplier?

A sole supplier is the only company that makes something you need. Imagine your cricket team's bats all use one special handle, and only one small shop in town makes that handle. If the shop owner stops selling, nobody plays, no matter how many bats are waiting.

That is exactly the trouble Boeing described. In its complaint, Boeing said Vaero was the sole supplier of the rib kit. There was no second shop to call.

The chain of companies that make and move the parts for a product is called a supply chain. Think of the milk, tea leaves, sugar and cups that reach a chai stall. If the milk van does not come, the stall cannot make chai, even if everything else is there.

How much does a stopped line cost?

Boeing's complaint said the disruption was costing it as much as $6.5 million a day. That is the top figure Boeing gave, not an exact daily bill.

Just to get a feel for the size: if that top figure held for 60 days, it would add up to $390 million. That is simple multiplication, not a number Boeing or any report has given for the full pause.

There was a deal. So why is the line still quiet?

The two companies reached a settlement in late September. A settlement is when both sides agree to end a court fight, a bit like two friends sorting out who owes whom for the pizza instead of fighting about it all week.

But even after that, three Boeing workers told Reuters that 777 freighter production has yet to resume. They did not give their names because they were not allowed to speak publicly. One worker said the 767 line has started getting some parts again since the deal.

Boeing declined to comment. Vaero did not answer requests for comment.

Half-built planes pushed aside

Without the Vaero parts, Boeing took two partly built 777 freighters off its final assembly line, one worker said. Reuters used data from aviation consultancy IBA to identify one of them as being built for FedEx, the US delivery giant. FedEx did not reply to Reuters.

Boeing has still delivered 21 777 freighters so far this year, company data show. Two workers said a handful more, whose wings were built before the fight began, could still be delivered before the year ends.

The newer 777X is not affected. Its wings are made of composite material, a light and strong mix of fibres, so they do not use this rib kit.

Why cargo planes matter so much

A freighter is a plane built to carry goods instead of passengers.

Boeing says its planes provide more than 90% of all global freighter capacity today. Capacity here means how much cargo all the planes together can carry. That is why a pause on a Boeing freighter line gets noticed.

The 767 matters too. FedEx is the largest operator of the 767-300 Freighter and has taken delivery of its 100th 767, Boeing says. The 767 freighter can carry a payload of 52,480 kg, which is the weight of the goods inside.

How did Boeing end up here?

For most of its history, Boeing built most of its plane parts itself. That changed in 2003 with the launch of the 787 Dreamliner programme, Mint reports. Boeing began buying parts from suppliers around the world to cut costs. Mint notes that this shift has been blamed for many of Boeing's recent troubles, including quality and safety concerns.

Buying parts from outside is called outsourcing. It is like a samosa stall that stops making its own chutney and buys it from a neighbour. It can be cheaper and faster, until the neighbour shuts the shop for a week.

Now Boeing is trying to bring the rib kit in-house, two people told Reuters. In-house means making it in its own factories, so it does not depend on one outside company again.

The big lesson

One small kit from one small company was enough to stop the line for a cargo plane that is still in strong demand. Reuters called it a sign of how fragile aerospace supply chains are. For anyone starting a business, even a small one, the lesson is simple: know which supplier you cannot live without, and have a plan for the day they stop picking up the phone.
